title: Strategy Is a Leadership Capability
author: Make Better Strategy
summary: This Make Better Strategy piece argues that what organizations diagnose as an 'execution problem' is almost always a leadership problem in disguise - and that reframing is good news, because a leadership problem is specific, locatable, and learnable, while 'execution problem' names a diffuse failure with no clear owner. The author defines strategic leadership as a concrete capability with five distinct faces: Lead (holding strategic direction continuously, not just at launch), Align (creating coherence across both vertical objectives and horizontal cross-team coordination, which most organizations get wrong because they align on paper while daily work stays pointed at the old strategy), Transform (building the organizational capacity the new strategy actually requires), Mobilize (getting people to believe in a strategy, not just be informed of it, since belief can't be cascaded and must be built by involving people), and Evaluate (treating strategy as a set of falsifiable bets and adapting early when some prove wrong). The piece insists these are not five separate initiatives to run in parallel but five dimensions of one capability to diagnose, and recommends a simple self-scoring exercise where the value lies not in the total score but in identifying the one dimension that lags far behind the others.
points: The article reframes 'execution problems' as leadership problems specifically because 'leadership' as defined here is a learnable capability, not a vague organizational failure with no fixable owner.

Strategy execution is broken into five distinct capabilities — Lead, Align, Transform, Mobilize, Evaluate — each of which can independently succeed or fail, producing different diagnosable failure modes.

The piece's key alignment insight is that most organizations align on paper while daily work stays pointed at the old strategy, and that alignment must also work horizontally across functions, not just vertically.
The self-scoring exercise (1-5 on each of the five dimensions) is framed as more useful for its shape — the one dimension scoring far below the others — than for the total score itself.
quotes: You don't have an execution problem. You have a leadership one.

Because "execution problem" is a dead end — it points at everyone and no one, at some diffuse failure of the organization to do the thing. "Leadership problem" is specific, locatable, and — crucially — learnable.

Most strategies get announced with real energy and then quietly drift because no one is holding the line week to week. Leading a strategy is less like firing a starting gun and more like keeping a heartbeat.
This is the one most organizations get wrong, because they align on paper (everyone's OKRs ladder up) while the actual daily work stays pointed at last year's strategy.
You cannot cascade belief. You have to build it, and you build it by involving people in the strategy rather than handing it down for implementation.
A strategy doesn't fail vaguely. It stops being lived somewhere specific.
A diagram is something you nod at. A diagnosis is something you act on.
